subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Ethiopian Coffee Ceremony
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Ethiopian Coffee Ceremony.

hook.text: In Ethiopia, coffee isn't just made—it's performed. The 'buna' ceremony takes up to an hour and involves three rounds.

buildup.text: Green beans are roasted in a pan over charcoal. The smoke is wafted toward guests as a fragrant welcome.

discovery.text: The roasted beans are ground by hand, brewed in a clay jebena pot, and poured from height into small cups.

twist.text: Three rounds must be served: abol, tona, and baraka. The third round is considered a blessing—leaving before it is rude.

climax.text: The ceremony is about community, not caffeine. It strengthens bonds between neighbors, families, and friends.

punchline.text: An hour for three cups. In Ethiopia, coffee is a relationship, not a rush.

quiz.question: How many rounds are served in an Ethiopian coffee ceremony?

details.summary: The Ethiopian coffee ceremony is a ritual lasting one to two hours where green beans are roasted, ground, and brewed in front of guests. Incense is burned, and coffee is served in three rounds of decreasing strength. It is a cornerstone of Ethiopian hospitality and social bonding.
details.whyItMatters: The Ethiopian ceremony represents coffee's deepest cultural roots. In the birthplace of coffee, drinking it remains a communal ritual, not a solo habit.
takeaways: The ceremony involves roasting green beans in front of guests
Coffee is served in three rounds of decreasing strength
It is a central ritual in Ethiopian social and family life

faq.question: What are the three rounds of the Ethiopian coffee ceremony?
faq.answer: The first round, abol, is the strongest. The second, tona, reuses the grounds and is milder. The third, baraka, meaning blessing, is the lightest. Completing all three rounds is considered a sign of respect. Leaving before the third round is impolite.

faq.question: What equipment is used in the Ethiopian ceremony?
faq.answer: A flat iron pan for roasting beans over charcoal. A wooden mortar and pestle for grinding. A jebena, a clay pot with a narrow neck, for brewing. Small handleless cups called sini for serving. Fresh grass is spread on the floor and incense is burned.
